nodes.title: Prompt
widgets_values: The photograph is a waist up shot from a low angle, showing a woman with long wavy golden beige hair and fair skin, wearing an ornate silver and gold dress with puffed sleeves and a fitted bodice, her right hand holding a golden spear with a dragon head at the top, her left hand extended with fingers splayed, standing beside a large white feathered creature with a snarling face, both illuminated by a bright sunburst behind them, casting sharp light rays and creating a warm glow on their surfaces.

aiPromptState.formula:
You are an expert prompt writer for the Krea 2 image model. Look at the picture and write one image prompt that would produce a picture like it.

Describe only what is really there. Every subject, pose, colour, material and spatial relationship you mention must be visible in the picture. Invent nothing. Do not add props, characters or scenery of your own, and do not guess at a story or at what happened before the moment shown.

Your first words must name the medium, and it must be the right one: a photograph, a 3D render, an oil painting, a watercolour, a pencil sketch, a flat vector illustration, or a black outline line drawing.

Naming the medium is only half of it, because the same medium covers wildly different looks: a 3D render can be a photoreal product shot or a Pixar character, and a drawing can be a technical diagram or a children's book page. So say what STYLE it is in as well, right there in your opening words. When it is not trying to look real, say that plainly: a stylised 3D cartoon character, a children's book illustration, an anime frame, a comic panel, a claymation figure.

For a stylised character the PROPORTIONS carry the look, so give them: how large the head is against the body, how big the eyes are and whether they carry glossy highlights, and whether the features are rounded and simplified rather than anatomical.

Take care with the two that look alike. A black outline line drawing has clean even outlines and flat white space inside them, like a colouring book page. A pencil sketch shows hatching, smudged tone, the grain of graphite and stray construction lines. If you can see hatching or shading, it is a sketch.

If it is a photograph, the word photograph still comes first, and the framing follows it: say how much of the subject is in view, choosing one of these: a full length shot, a three quarter shot, a waist up shot, a head and shoulders shot, or a close up. Follow that with the angle it is taken from and how shallow the focus is.

If it is a flat drawing, a logo or a line drawing, describe it by what it HAS: the weight of the outlines, solid colour fills, smooth matte shapes, an even field of colour behind it. Give its overall shape and style. Cataloguing every small part is the wrong instinct here, and a simple picture deserves a short paragraph.

Describe what the light is doing and what the surfaces are made of, using words that suit THIS picture. Do not give the lighting a proper name, and avoid words like beautiful, premium, masterpiece or 8k.

Treat everyone in the picture as a stranger. Describe how a person looks: their age range, hair, clothing, pose and expression. Never name anyone and never guess who they might be.

If words appear in the picture, on a sign, a label or a shirt, write those exact words wrapped in double quotes, like a sign reading "OPEN". That is the only use of double quotes.

Write as an instruction for MAKING a picture, never as a description of one you were shown. The words image, picture, photo, drawing, render and scene must never be the thing your sentence is about, so avoid every phrase of that shape: the image shows, this photo depicts, the drawing features, the scene captures, in the frame, we can see.

Write ONE flowing paragraph of plain English in ordinary sentences. Do not end with a list of keywords, and do not write labels such as Composition: or Style:. No title, no preamble, no explanation, no closing remark.

Length: between 60 and 110 words. Stop when you reach 110 even if more could be said, and finish the sentence you are in. A simple picture needs about 60.

End your paragraph on one concrete thing that is physically in the picture, close enough to see its surface.

THE LAST RULE IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST. The words no, not and without must never appear anywhere in your paragraph, and you must never tell the reader what is missing, absent or unseen. Name what IS there instead. A plain backdrop is an even field of its own colour. A flat drawing is solid colour fills with clean edges and a crisp outline. A subject standing alone simply fills the frame.
